knowledge_points.label: Collectives: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather
knowledge_points.statement: The multi-GPU building blocks are reduce, all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast and reduce-scatter; an all-reduce can be implemented as a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, and in the bandwidth-limited regime that two-step decomposition is the best you can do.

anchors.quote: Reduce ... All reduce ... All Gather ... Broadcast ... Reduce Scatter
Reduce can be implemented as two steps: reduce-scatter and all-gather
Importantly, in the bandwidth-limited regime, this is the best you can do
We're going to be dealing with this at the level of collective communication primitives. ... But our discussion today is going to be algorithmic.
the equivalence between all-reduce and reduce-scatter plus all-gather. ... And the fact that these two have the same cost in some sense means that we can do the algorithm on the right for free.
Yes, yes, there are other decompositions. ... This one in particular will be useful for a algorithm, which is why I'm emphasizing this particular decomposition.

provenance.filtering_note: Slide p7 is five diagrams with only their names in the text layer; the per-rank byte counts (an all-reduce of N bytes over M ranks moves about 2N(M-1)/M per rank) are never written in this deck. Slide p8's title says 'all reduce vs reduce-scatter-gather' while its first bullet says 'Reduce can be implemented...'; the figure shows the all-reduce decomposition. The executable lecture 7 (collective_operations section) is where the primitives are run in code. Spoken evidence (3:14-3:38): the professor singles out the decomposition as the one fact needed later: because a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather costs the same as one all-reduce, 'we can do the algorithm on the right for free' (used for ZeRO stage 1 at 18:25-18:56). In Q&A (4:07-4:17) he adds that other decompositions exist and this one is emphasized only because the ZeRO algorithm needs it. The whole lecture stays at the level of collectives ('our discussion today is going to be algorithmic', 3:05); hardware-level implementation is skipped (see spoken_filtering). No per-rank byte count is said aloud either.

external_prerequisites.note: Lecture 7 runs reduce-scatter / all-gather with torch.distributed and shows the all-reduce decomposition in code.

misconceptions.belief: Reduce-scatter plus all-gather is a slower, two-hop way to do what all-reduce does in one shot.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In the bandwidth-limited regime the decomposition is bandwidth-optimal: it is how ring all-reduce is implemented, and splitting it lets ZeRO insert a local update between the two halves at no extra cost.

predict.q: An all-reduce of the gradient vector across 8 GPUs is replaced by a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, with nothing else changed. In the bandwidth-limited regime, how does total communication change?
choices: about 2x more
about the same

predict.why: Slide p8: an all-reduce can be implemented as exactly these two steps, and that implementation is already the best you can do when bandwidth is the limit. The decomposition exposes a seam, it does not add traffic.
predict.targets_misconception: Reduce-scatter plus all-gather is a slower, two-hop way to do what all-reduce does in one shot.

transfer.q: After the reduce-scatter step each rank holds the fully summed gradient for its own 1/M slice of the parameters. If each rank only ever needs to update its own slice, which half of the all-reduce decomposition can be skipped, and which collective is still needed afterwards to let everyone see the new parameters?
transfer.answer: Skip the all-gather of gradients; after the local update, all-gather the parameters instead.
transfer.why: This is exactly the ZeRO stage 1 schedule (p20): reduce-scatter gradients, update locally, all-gather parameters, so the two halves of the all-reduce are kept but the second one carries parameters rather than gradients.

check.q: Eight GPUs each hold a full gradient vector. Rank 3 has just finished a reduce-scatter(SUM) of the gradients. What does rank 3 now hold?
choices: All entries, from its own gradient only
All entries, summed over all 8 ranks
Its 1/8 slice, from its own gradient only
Its 1/8 slice, summed over all 8 ranks
check.answer: Its 1/8 slice, summed over all 8 ranks
check.why: Reduce-scatter leaves each rank with the full reduction of its own 1/M slice; an all-gather of those slices is what turns it into an all-reduce (p8). That is why ZeRO can stop after the reduce-scatter and update only its slice.
check.varies: asks what one half of the decomposition leaves on a rank, instead of which half the ZeRO schedule can skip
check.invariant: all-reduce = reduce-scatter (each rank owns one fully reduced slice) + all-gather (every rank gets every slice)
distractor_from: 'All entries, summed over all 8 ranks' <- misconception: 'Reduce-scatter plus all-gather is a slower, two-hop way to do what all-reduce does in one shot' (treats the first hop as already the whole all-reduce)
'Its 1/8 slice, from its own gradient only' <- plausible: a scatter without the reduce
'All entries, from its own gradient only' <- plausible: thinks nothing has been communicated yet
check.targets_misconception: Reduce-scatter plus all-gather is a slower, two-hop way to do what all-reduce does in one shot.

retrieval.answer: Reduce-scatter, then all-gather.

retrieval.answer: The bandwidth-limited regime.

knowledge_points.label: Bandwidth hierarchy: intra-node interconnect vs inter-node network
knowledge_points.statement: GPUs inside a node talk over high-speed interconnects (all-to-all, up to 8 GPUs per node on GPUs; TPUs use a toroidal mesh), nodes talk over a slower network, and the whole datacenter is the new unit of compute; which link a parallelism scheme stresses decides where it is placed.

anchors.quote: Intra-node parallelism ... High-speed inter-node parallelism ... via high-speed interconnects ... Split up memory and compute requirements across GPUs and machines
TPU networking toroidal mesh ... GPU networking All-to-all (up to 256)
Pro mesh – Cheaper to operate, can be made fast (and just do tensor parallel) ... Pro tree/A2A – Better for less structured communications (expert parallel)
On GPUs, tensor parallel within a node (up to 8 GPUs) due to high speed interconnects.
New unit of compute – the datacenter

the difference between intranode parallelism, where your connections are very fast, and so you can do things that are very communication expensive. ... And you're going to have slower internode communication.

the TPU network is what's called a toroidal mesh. ... All the chips are networked to neighbors and the neighbors wrap around ... The number of neighbors you have is the same, no matter how large your network gets.
the GPU networking philosophy is very different. It's really much more of an all to all philosophy. ... It's often called a fat tree.
if you're communicating only to neighbors, TPUs are great. ... But if you're connecting in very random ways, very stochastic, unpredictable ways, then this GPU networking will be more flexible

That's a tree topology. They've switched to a much more all to all connection. ... a little bit of a convergent evolution across both TPUs and GPUs, where really the workloads are defining the network that we need to have.
each chip is a lot worse than a H200. ... like in their case, 384 in a big rack ... It's four times that of the equivalent NVIDIA system.
the new unit of compute is not the GPU. It's the entire data center.

provenance.filtering_note: All bandwidth numbers are figure-only. p9 pastes the NVIDIA SuperPOD table (A100 vs H100: 1 DGX bisection 2,400 vs 3,600 GB/s, 32 DGXs 6,400 vs 57,600 GB/s, i.e. '9x' bisection speedup; reduce 150/450 and 100/450 GB/s). p12 pastes the SemiAnalysis GB200 NVL72 vs CloudMatrix 384 table (scale-up domain 72 vs 384 GPUs; scale-up bandwidth 518,400 vs 1,075,200 GB/s uni-di; scale-out 28,800 vs 153,600 GB/s) with only the title and URL in the text layer. p11 (TPU8i/t 'Virgo' switched networks) is an aside. The deck never states a GB/s figure for NVLink vs InfiniBand in text; the qualitative ordering fast-inside-node, slower-between-nodes is what the later placement rules (p35, p42, p57) rest on. Spoken evidence (5:37-6:43): the reason for each topology. A torus keeps the neighbour count constant 'no matter how large your network gets', so it scales simply and each link can be made 'more beefy' for the same power; a fat tree costs more as it grows but suits 'random ... unpredictable' traffic such as MoE token routing (7:10, Dally and Dean). TPU8i is read aloud as a switch to 'a tree topology' for MoE serving, 'convergent evolution' driven by workloads (7:42-8:43). Huawei CloudMatrix 384 (9:14-10:26): each chip 'a lot worse than a H200', 384 per rack over optical switches, at 'four times' the power of the NVIDIA system; these are readings of the p12 SemiAnalysis table (figure-only) and were not checked against it. He rounds the domain to 'scale out much more aggressively to 300 chips' (10:02), against 384 on the slide; not imported. No GB/s figure is said aloud. The mesh-vs-tree theme returns at 43:26 (TPUs can run much larger tensor parallel) and 1:16:36 (Gemma 2 without pipelines).

misconceptions.belief: A cluster of 256 GPUs is one big GPU; any pair of GPUs can exchange data at the same speed.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only GPUs inside a node share the high-speed all-to-all interconnect (up to 8 on standard GPU nodes); crossing nodes drops to the network, which is why the deck says to tensor-parallel within a node and pipeline across nodes.

predict.q: You have 16 GPUs in two 8-GPU nodes. A scheme needs every GPU to exchange activations with every other GPU many times per layer. Where does the deck say the slow part is?
choices: inside each node, between the 8 GPUs
between the two nodes
equally everywhere
predict.why: Intra-node GPUs sit on a high-speed interconnect (all-to-all, up to 8); inter-node traffic crosses the slower network. That asymmetry is the whole reason parallelism types are assigned to levels.
predict.targets_misconception: A cluster of 256 GPUs is one big GPU; any pair of GPUs can exchange data at the same speed.

transfer.q: Slide 10 says a mesh is good when 'you just do tensor parallel' and a tree / all-to-all is 'better for less structured communications (expert parallel)'. A new MoE training job routes tokens to arbitrary experts on arbitrary chips. Which topology does the deck's reasoning favour, and what property of the traffic drives the choice?
transfer.answer: Tree / all-to-all; the traffic is unstructured (any chip to any chip), whereas a mesh suits the regular neighbour-to-neighbour pattern of tensor parallel.
transfer.why: Tensor parallel's all-reduces are regular and can be made fast on a cheap mesh; expert routing produces irregular all-to-all dispatch, which needs a switched topology (slide 11 even notes TPU8i moving closer to tree-style 'maybe for MoEs').

a tree / all-to-all
a mesh (toroidal)

check.varies: the traffic pattern (regular TP all-reduces instead of irregular MoE routing), so the answer flips
check.invariant: the structure of the traffic, not the model, decides which topology fits
distractor_from: 'a tree / all-to-all' <- plausible: carries the MoE answer over without checking the traffic pattern
'no difference: all links equal' <- misconception: 'A cluster of 256 GPUs is one big GPU; any pair of GPUs can exchange data at the same speed.'
check.targets_misconception: A cluster of 256 GPUs is one big GPU; any pair of GPUs can exchange data at the same speed.

retrieval.answer: TPU: toroidal mesh. GPU: all-to-all (up to 256).

knowledge_points.label: Naive data parallel: compute B/M, comm 2x params, memory none
knowledge_points.statement: Splitting a batch of B across M machines and exchanging gradients gives each GPU B/M examples (linear compute scaling), costs 2x #params of communication per batch (fine when batches are big), and gives no memory scaling because every GPU still holds all parameters.

anchors.quote: Naive parallelism: split the elements of B sized batch across M machines. Exchange gradients to synchronize
Compute scaling – each GPU gets B/M examples. ... Communication overhead – transmits 2x # params every batch. OK if batches are big ... Memory scaling – none. Every GPU needs # params at least
Linear memory scaling (max model params scales with num gpus) ... Linear compute scaling (model flops scale linearly with num gpus)
take my batch, B. I can cut it up across M machines. ... each machine computes gradients, and then I will synchronize all the gradients to get my sum.

So compute scaling wise, this is perfect. As long as there's enough examples per GPU, we're good. ... every batch, we have to basically communicate two times the number of parameters ... And then for memory scaling, there's absolutely none.

provenance.filtering_note: The '2x # params' is stated as a count in parameter units, not bytes; the deck never multiplies by the gradient dtype. It is the ring all-reduce cost (each parameter leaves and re-enters each GPU once), stated here as given, derived nowhere in the deck. 'OK if batches are big' is the first appearance of the compute/communication ratio idea: communication is fixed per step while compute grows with B/M. Spoken evidence (12:47-13:10): the three lines of p15 read aloud; 'As long as there's enough examples per GPU' is the spoken form of 'OK if batches are big'. The 2x is explained only as 'communicate my gradients back and forth' (13:00), not derived. Spoken imprecision (13:13): 'You need to have the same sized activations so you don't save any memory' holds at a fixed per-GPU batch; at a fixed global batch each GPU's activations shrink with B/M. Not imported; the statement's claim (parameters are not split) is unaffected.

Per-rank byte counts of the collectives, which this deck states only as 2x / 3x #params and 8bsh(n-1)/n.

misconceptions.belief: Adding more data-parallel GPUs lets you train a bigger model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Naive data parallel copies the full model to every GPU; it scales compute and batch size, not the maximum model size. Memory scaling needs ZeRO or model parallelism.

choices: drops to about 1/8
unchanged
grows by 2x because of gradient buffers
predict.why: Slide 15: 'Memory scaling – none. Every GPU needs # params at least.' Each replica holds a full copy of parameters, gradients and optimizer state; only the batch is divided.
predict.targets_misconception: Adding more data-parallel GPUs lets you train a bigger model.

transfer.q: Using the deck's accounting, a 70B-parameter model trained with naive data parallel on a global batch of 1024 sequences across 16 GPUs (the deck's 'machines', one GPU each): how many examples does each GPU process per step, and how many parameter-units of communication does each step cost?
transfer.answer: 64 examples per GPU (1024/16); 2 x 70B = 140B parameter-units of communication per step.
transfer.why: Compute scales as B/M and communication is a fixed 2x #params per batch regardless of batch size, which is why the deck says the overhead is 'OK if batches are big': doubling B doubles compute per step but leaves communication unchanged.

check.q: Using the deck's accounting (communication = 2 × #params per step), a 7B-parameter model trained with naive data parallel on 32 GPUs doubles its global batch from 512 to 1024 sequences. How many billion parameter-units of communication does each step cost after the change?
check.why: Communication is 2 × 7B = 14B parameter-units per step whatever the batch size; doubling B doubles each GPU's compute (512/32 = 16 to 1024/32 = 32 examples) but not the gradient exchange, which is why the overhead is 'OK if batches are big' (p15).
check.varies: model size, GPU count, and the change made (batch doubled) instead of a fresh configuration
check.invariant: compute per GPU scales as B/M; communication is a fixed 2 × #params per step

retrieval.answer: 2x #params.

steps.do: Compute: split the batch of B examples across M GPUs; each runs forward and backward on B/M of them.
steps.why: A GPU's work is proportional to the examples it sees, so compute per GPU falls as 1/M: linear compute scaling, as long as each GPU still has enough examples.

steps.do: Communication: all-reduce the gradients, a reduce-scatter (#params) plus an all-gather (#params), so 2 × #params per batch.
steps.why: Each GPU computed its gradient on different examples, so the sum must be exchanged once per step. The count depends only on the parameter count, not on B, which is why the deck says it is 'OK if batches are big'.

steps.do: Memory: every GPU still holds all parameters, gradients and optimizer state. For the 7B model on 8 GPUs, the per-GPU parameter-related memory is unchanged.
steps.why: Only the batch is divided; the model is replicated on every GPU, so there is no memory scaling.

knowledge_points.label: Mixed-precision Adam needs 16 bytes/param (12 with BF16 moments)
knowledge_points.statement: Training with BF16 compute and Adam keeps 5 copies of the weights worth of state: 2 bytes BF16 parameters + 2 bytes BF16 gradients + 4 bytes FP32 master weights + 4 + 4 bytes FP32 Adam moments = 16 bytes per parameter, or 12 bytes if the moments are kept in BF16.

anchors.quote: We need 5 copies of weights and 16 bytes per param!

2 bytes for FP/BF 16 model parameters ... 2 bytes for FP/BF 16 gradients ... 4 bytes for FP32 master weights (the thing you accumulate into in SGD) ... 4 (or 2) bytes for FP32/BF16 Adam first moment estimates ... 4 (or 2) bytes for FP32/BF16 Adam second moment estimates
Pure BF16 training (with Kahan summation), is viable and optimizer states are less beefy. Let’s say BF16 for everything but the master weights – 12 bytes per param
But the rule of thumb, you might say, is that we need something like five copies of weights and 16 bytes per parameter to store our model.

You might need to have a higher precision accumulator that you accumulate into in SGD. ... And if you're doing Adam, and this is really where the bad stuff comes in ... you might need to store them in high precision depending on your stability characteristics.
If you look at the accounting, this is most of the cost memory wise of doing an SGD update.

provenance.filtering_note: The deck labels the two Adam moments '"Optimizer state"' and groups the master weights separately, but in the ZeRO memory formula (p21) K counts everything beyond the 2+2 bytes of parameters and gradients, so K = 12 for the p17 ledger. Activation memory is explicitly excluded until p44. Kahan summation (p28) is named but not explained. Spoken evidence (14:21-15:04): whether the Adam moments need FP32 depends on 'your stability characteristics' (the slide gives '4 (or 2)' without a reason), and the optimizer state (accumulator plus two moments, 12 of the 16 bytes) is 'most of the cost memory wise'. He calls the FP32 master copy an accumulator that 'might be temporary' (14:26).

misconceptions.belief: A BF16 model costs 2 bytes per parameter to train, so a 40B model fits in 80 GB.
misconceptions.why_wrong: 2 bytes is the inference footprint. Training adds gradients, FP32 master weights and two Adam moments: 16 bytes/param (12 with BF16 moments), so 40B needs 640 GB (or 480 GB) before activations.

predict.targets_misconception: A BF16 model costs 2 bytes per parameter to train, so a 40B model fits in 80 GB.

transfer.q: Same 13B model, but following slide 28 the Adam moments are stored in BF16 while master weights stay FP32. Bytes per parameter, and total GB?
transfer.why: 2 (params) + 2 (grads) + 4 (master) + 2 + 2 (BF16 moments) = 12; 12 x 13B = 156 GB. Only the two moment copies shrink; the master weights must stay FP32 to accumulate small updates.

check.varies: model size and the question direction (GPU count from total state, not state from model size)
check.invariant: BF16 + Adam training holds 16 bytes per parameter (5 weight-sized copies)
check.targets_misconception: A BF16 model costs 2 bytes per parameter to train, so a 40B model fits in 80 GB.

retrieval.q: List the five per-parameter copies in the deck's 16-byte training ledger with their byte counts.
retrieval.answer: BF16 params 2, BF16 grads 2, FP32 master weights 4, FP32 Adam first moment 4, FP32 Adam second moment 4.

prompts.self_explain: Why must the master weights, but not the gradients, be kept in FP32 even when everything else is BF16?

steps.do: BF16 parameters (2 bytes) plus BF16 gradients (2 bytes).
steps.why: The forward and backward passes compute in BF16, so the weights they read and the gradients they write are kept at 2 bytes.

steps.do: FP32 master weights: 4 bytes.
steps.why: The update is accumulated into an FP32 copy ('the thing you accumulate into in SGD'), because small updates would round away in BF16.

steps.do: FP32 Adam first and second moments: 4 + 4 = 8 bytes.
steps.why: Adam keeps two running statistics per parameter, each as large as the FP32 master copy.

steps.do: Sum the five weight-sized copies and multiply by the 13B parameters.
steps.why: The BF16 weights are only 2 of the 16 bytes (1/8 of the bill); activations come on top of this.

knowledge_points.label: ZeRO stage 1 and 2: shard optimizer state, then gradients, for free
knowledge_points.statement: ZeRO stage 1 splits optimizer state across GPUs and replaces DDP's gradient all-reduce by reduce-scatter(gradients) + local update + all-gather(parameters), keeping communication at 2x #params while memory falls from (4+K) to (4+K/N_gpu) bytes per param; stage 2 also keeps gradients sharded by reducing each layer's gradient to its owner and freeing it as the backward pass proceeds, again at 2x #params.

anchors.quote: Core idea: split up the expensive parts (state) and use the reduce-scatter equivalence.
Split up the optimizer state (first + second moments) across GPUs ... Everyone has the parameters + gradients
Step 2. ReduceScatter the gradients – incur #params communication cost ... Step 4. All Gather the parameters – incur #params communication cost
Communication cost 2* # params 2* # params ... Memory (4+K) * #params (4+K/Ngpu) * #params
ZeRO stage 1 is free (in the bandwidth limited regime) memory wins
Step 1a. After computing a layer’s gradients, immediately reduce to send this to the right worker ... Step 1b. Once gradients are not needed in the backward graph, immediately free it.
Zero stage 1 is 2*# param – it’s free! – you might as well always do it ... Zero stage 2 is 2*# param – it’s (almost) free (ignoring overhead)
the optimizer state is most of your memory. So here, the optimizer state is green. ... And notice how parameters and gradients are the same size, and your state is bigger
the implied memory gains on the very right would be quite dramatic as we go all the way down from 120 to 1.9.
I'm going to reduce scatter the gradients onto all the other machines. ... But they don't need all the gradients. They only need the gradients associated with their update.

knowledge_points.statement: Cutting a model into n stages by layer leaves each GPU active only 1/n of the time; pipeline parallel feeds m micro-batches so stages overlap, leaving a bubble whose ratio to useful compute is (n_stages-1)/n_micro, so big batches (many micro-batches) are needed to hide it.

knowledge_points.label: Global batch is one budget: data-parallel replicas and pipeline micro-batches share it
knowledge_points.statement: The global batch size is a resource that data parallelism and pipelining both spend: at a fixed global batch of B sequences, micro-batch size b and d data-parallel replicas, each pipeline gets n_micro = B/(d*b) micro-batches, so adding replicas enlarges the (n_stages-1)/n_micro bubble; and B cannot simply be raised to compensate, because past the critical batch size an extra example is worth less than an extra optimizer step.

anchors.quote: data parallel is consuming an important resource. And that resource is the batch size, so to speak ... If you have a batch size of 8, you can never have more than eight accelerators
there's something called the critical batch size, where the basically gain that you get from the additional batch element is less than if you had taken another SGD step on that single element
This is why I said batch sizes are useful resource. Because now we can spend it in a different way, which is to pipeline more to reduce the amount of idle time in pipeline parallel.
It consumes your global batch size in order to do parallelization. ... Maybe you want to do some tensor parallel to cut down on activation memory. It also doesn't touch global batch size.
With data parallel, #machines < batch size (and near this, comm overhead is high) ... And there’s diminishing returns to batch sizes
The ratio of bubble time to useful compute is .. ... so we need a big batch size!

The slides never connect the two. The table's 'Scales global batch?' column is the only written trace. The formula n_micro = B/(d*b) and all numbers in the prompts are the author's, following the Narayanan et al. 2021 accounting (megatron_ptd_p_2021); the critical-batch definition is the professor's (29:30-29:57). His slip in the same stretch (utilization as 'number of stages divided by this micro-batches', 33:41) is recorded under pipeline-bubble and not used here.

misconceptions.why_wrong: At a fixed global batch, each extra replica takes a share of the same sequences, so every pipeline gets fewer micro-batches and its (n_stages-1)/n_micro bubble grows.

misconceptions.belief: If the pipeline bubble is too large, just raise the global batch until it disappears.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Past the critical batch size an extra example in the batch gains less than an extra optimizer step on it, so a larger global batch buys utilization at the cost of optimization progress per example.

With 16 data-parallel replicas each pipeline gets 32 micro-batches, so the bubble ratio (n_stages-1)/n_micro is 7/32, about 0.22. You buy 4x more GPUs and use them all as extra data-parallel replicas (64 in total), keeping the global batch at 512. What is the new bubble ratio?
predict.why: Each of the 64 replicas now gets 512/64 = 8 micro-batches, so the bubble ratio is 7/8 = 0.875: four times larger. The batch that data parallelism spends is the same batch the pipeline needed to hide its bubble.
predict.targets_misconception: Data parallelism and pipeline parallelism are independent axes: adding data-parallel replicas never changes pipeline efficiency.

transfer.q: The critical batch size caps your global batch at 1,024 sequences. The model needs 16 pipeline stages to fit, and the micro-batch size is 1. You want the bubble ratio (n_stages-1)/n_micro to be at most 0.25. What is the largest power-of-two data-parallel degree you can use, and what does that imply for how many GPUs (pipeline x data) the job can usefully occupy?

So at most 16 x 16 = 256 GPUs (times any tensor-parallel degree); more GPUs would break either the batch cap or the bubble target.

With B capped by the critical batch size and n_micro forced up by the bubble target, the data-parallel degree, and with it the GPU count, is capped too. That is why the recipe adds tensor or expert parallelism (which do not consume the batch) before scaling further.

retrieval.answer: Each replica gets fewer sequences, so each pipeline gets fewer micro-batches (n_micro = B/(d*b)) and its bubble (n_stages-1)/n_micro grows.

knowledge_points.label: Tensor parallel: column/row matmul split, f and g collectives
knowledge_points.statement: Tensor parallel cuts a layer along its width: with A split by columns (A1, A2) and B by rows (B1, B2) on different GPUs, the forward pass needs f = identity before A and g = all-reduce after B, the backward pass swaps them; in a Transformer block QKV and the up-projection are column-split, attention output and the down-projection are row-split, and norms and routers are replicated.

anchors.quote: We can think of pipeline parallel as cutting up along depth. What about width? ... Simple matrix multiplication observation: decompose into submatrices, add partial sums
Assign columns (A1, A2) and rows (B1, B2) to separate GPUs. ... In the forward pass, f is the identity, and g is an all-reduce. ... In the backward pass, f is an all-reduce, g is the identity.
Columnwise – QKV, up-projection ... Rowwise – Attention output, down-projection ... Replicated – norms, routers, etc

anchors.ref: Megatron-LM Fig. 3 (MLP block with f and g)

anchors.quote: So pipeline parallel is like depth. ... So what if we start cutting up our model along width, right? So this is tensor parallel
matrix multiplies can be cut up into smaller matrix multiplies, which you then add the partial sums back together. This is really the same idea as tiling as well.
So in the forward pass, all I do with the x is I copy them twice ... So f is the identity, this f function. ... the g function, that's an all-reduce that brings them back together
But in the backwards pass, as I'm doing my gradients, this is going to flip. ... And this duality is important if you're going to write tensor parallel.

everything that's a small layer, like a layer norm or a non-linearity or routers ... those are all fully replicated across the machines. You don't really want to bother with the overhead of cutting those guys.

provenance.filtering_note: The p40 figure is Megatron-LM's MLP diagram: Y = GeLU(XA), Z = Dropout(YB); the GeLU sits between the column-split and row-split matmuls so each GPU can apply it to its own Y_i without communication (GeLU is elementwise), which the slide text does not spell out. Why the pairing is column-then-row (so the single all-reduce lands only after B) is implied by 'add partial sums'. The attention analogue (heads split across GPUs) is only named on p41. Spoken evidence (41:07-41:31): why the backward flips. The partial derivatives arrive whole at g (identity), and the partials must be summed at f; 'this duality is important if you're going to write tensor parallel'. Small layers are replicated because cutting them is not worth the overhead (42:16). The width split is 'the same idea as tiling' (39:58; lecture 5). The GeLU-locality point is not said aloud either.

external_prerequisites.note: Lecture 7 implements the column/row split in code.

misconceptions.belief: Splitting both matmuls of an MLP across 2 GPUs requires an all-reduce after each matmul.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Column-splitting A yields full-height slices Y1, Y2 that the elementwise GeLU can process independently; row-splitting B then produces partial sums that need just one all-reduce (g). One collective per MLP in forward, one (f) in backward.

predict.q: In the Megatron MLP on slide 40 (Y = GeLU(XA), Z = Dropout(YB)) spread over 2 GPUs, how many all-reduces happen in the forward pass?
predict.why: f is the identity in forward (X is simply used by both GPUs) and only g, after the row-split B, is an all-reduce that sums the partial Y_i B_i. The backward pass mirrors this with f becoming the all-reduce.
predict.targets_misconception: Splitting both matmuls of an MLP across 2 GPUs requires an all-reduce after each matmul.

transfer.q: Someone proposes splitting A by rows and B by columns instead. Using the slide-39 observation ('decompose into submatrices, add partial sums'), where would the communication now have to happen, and why is that worse than column-then-row?
transfer.answer: Row-splitting A makes each GPU produce a partial sum of XA that must be all-reduced before the GeLU (GeLU of a sum is not the sum of GeLUs), and column-splitting B then needs an all-gather to assemble Z: two collectives per MLP instead of one.
transfer.why: The column-then-row order places the one unavoidable reduction after the last matmul and keeps the nonlinearity local; reversing it inserts a reduction in front of the nonlinearity.

check.q: Megatron MLP on 2 GPUs: A split by columns, B by rows, Y = GeLU(XA), Z = Dropout(YB). In the backward pass, where does the single all-reduce happen?
choices: Nowhere: backward needs none
At g, on the gradient w.r.t. Z
After both the A and B gradients
At f, on the gradient w.r.t. X
check.answer: At f, on the gradient w.r.t. X
check.why: f is identity in forward and all-reduce in backward; g is the reverse (p40). Each GPU's dL/dX through its column-slice of A is a partial sum, so the sum over GPUs happens at f, before the gradient leaves the MLP.
check.varies: the backward pass instead of the split layout of the forward pass
check.invariant: the all-reduce sits wherever per-GPU partial sums must be combined: after B in forward, at the input X in backward
distractor_from: 'At g, on the gradient w.r.t. Z' <- plausible: assumes backward reuses the forward placement instead of swapping f and g
'After both the A and B gradients' <- misconception: 'Splitting both matmuls of an MLP across 2 GPUs requires an all-reduce after each matmul.'
'Nowhere: backward needs none' <- plausible: reads f = identity in forward as 'f never communicates'
check.targets_misconception: Splitting both matmuls of an MLP across 2 GPUs requires an all-reduce after each matmul.

retrieval.q: In the forward pass of a tensor-parallel MLP, which of f and g is the identity and which is an all-reduce?
retrieval.answer: f is the identity, g is an all-reduce (reversed in backward).

retrieval.q: Which Transformer matrices are split columnwise and which rowwise under tensor parallel?
retrieval.answer: Columnwise: QKV and the up-projection. Rowwise: attention output and the down-projection. Norms and routers are replicated.

prompts.self_explain: Why can the GeLU be applied to each GPU's slice without communication, but the dropout only after the all-reduce?

steps.do: f in forward is the identity: both GPUs take the full input X.
steps.why: With A split by columns, each GPU needs every input feature, and X is already present on both, so nothing is sent.

steps.do: Each GPU computes its own column slice of the hidden layer.
steps.why: GeLU is elementwise, so each GPU can apply it to its slice without first summing anything.

steps.do: Each GPU multiplies its slice by its row block B_i and gets a partial sum of Z.
steps.why: Row-splitting B matches the column split of Y: each GPU owns the rows of B that multiply its columns of Y.

steps.do: g in forward is an all-reduce: the two partial sums are added, so both GPUs hold Z. That is one all-reduce in the forward pass.
steps.why: The only sum the computation needs comes after the last matmul ('decompose into submatrices, add partial sums').

steps.do: In a Transformer block, QKV and the up-projection play the role of the column-split A; the attention output and down-projection are the row-split B; norms and routers are replicated.
steps.why: Each sublayer becomes one column-then-row pair, so each pays a single all-reduce; small per-token ops are cheaper to replicate than to split.

knowledge_points.label: TP vs PP: 8bsh(n-1)/n all-reduce per layer vs bsh point-to-point
knowledge_points.statement: Pipeline parallel sends b*s*h activations point-to-point per micro-batch between adjacent stages, while tensor parallel moves 8*b*s*h*(n_devices-1)/n_devices per layer in blocking all-reduces; tensor parallel has no bubble, is simple to wrap and needs no large batch, but its much larger communication confines it to low-latency high-bandwidth intra-node links, with pipeline parallel on the slower inter-node links.

anchors.quote: Pros – no bubble. If your network is fast enough, there’s no waiting for others. ... low complexity – simple to ‘wrap’ models without major infra changes ... doesn’t need large batch sizes to work well
Cons – much larger communication than pipeline parallel. ... Pipeline: ... point-to-point communication per microbatch ... Tensor: 8 ... per layer and all-reduce communication.
Use tensor parallel whenever we have low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects
Pipelines save memory (compared to DDP) ... Pipelines can have good communication properties (compared to FDSP) – it depends only on activations ... and is point to point
Generally, we will use pipelines on slower network links (i.e. inter-node) as a way to get better memory-wise scaling.
On GPUs, tensor parallel within a node (up to 8 GPUs) due to high speed interconnects.
So why do we do pipeline parallel? Well, pipelines can save memory compared to DDP. ... It only depends on activations, like b times s times h. It is also point to point.

pipelines are going to live on the slowest networking links. So if you have multiple data centers or multiple pods that are slower to talk to, you're going to parallelize across those two using pipelined parallel

It's a smaller amount of stuff that's being communicated. So it's batch times sequence length times hidden. And that's almost always a smaller amount of data than attempting to communicate a whole parameter matrix
Tensor parallel is extremely computation hungry. ... So this is very communication hungry. And so you only want to do this within a node.
And so up to eight, you might be willing to do some tensor parallel. ... you're going to get a big drop in performance as soon as you hit that point of going beyond a single machine.
for TPUs, you don't really have this distinction between fast eight GPUs and next machines. ... you can tensor parallel very large numbers compared to the GPU world

It used to be that you were doing b times s times h point to point communication. Now instead, I'm going to be doing something like a times b times s times h times roughly one all-reduce communication

provenance.filtering_note: The symbols bsh and the fraction (n_devices-1)/n_devices are math-italic images on p43 and p35, absent from the text layer (only the '8' survives). The 8 is not derived: it is 2 all-reduces per layer (attention + MLP) x 2 (forward + backward) x 2 (the all-reduce moves about 2x the tensor), each over a bsh activation. Per-step totals are not given; TP's cost is per layer while PP's is per stage boundary, so with forward and backward counted on both sides the per-step ratio is 8bsh(n-1)/n x (n x L) / (2bsh(n-1)) = 4L, with L layers per stage (author correction 2026-10-02; an earlier note gave 8 L (n-1)/n). The p55 recap table restates the comparison qualitatively (pipeline: 'Activation traffic between stages', tensor: 'Activation-sized collectives every block'). Spoken evidence: why pipeline traffic is small. It is 'batch times sequence length times hidden', 'almost always a smaller amount of data than ... a whole parameter matrix' (36:19-36:35, Q&A). Pipelines go on the slowest links, including across pods or data centers (35:01-35:22). On TPUs the mesh removes the 8-GPU boundary, so 'you can tensor parallel very large numbers' and the TP/PP mix differs from GPUs (43:31-43:57; slide p10's 'just do tensor parallel'). Self-corrected in the talk: 'extremely computation hungry' (42:26) becomes 'very communication hungry' (42:48). Caption or slip (44:33): 'a times b times s times h', where p43 says 8bsh(n-1)/n; probably 'eight' mis-captioned. Not imported. The 8 is still not derived aloud.

external_prerequisites.note: Per-rank byte counts of the collectives, which this deck states only as 2x / 3x #params and 8bsh(n-1)/n.

misconceptions.belief: Tensor parallel is the better scheme in every respect since it has no bubble; pipeline parallel is a fallback for people who cannot wrap their model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: TP pays roughly 8bsh(n-1)/n of all-reduce traffic per layer, blocking, versus one bsh point-to-point hop per stage boundary for PP. Over a slow inter-node link TP's blocking collectives stall every layer, while PP's cost is small and hideable; that is why TP stays inside the node.

predict.q: A model with 32 layers is split either as 8-way tensor parallel or 8-way pipeline parallel (4 layers per stage). Per forward+backward of one micro-batch, roughly how many times more activation-sized traffic does TP move than PP, using the slide-43 formulas (TP: 8bsh(n−1)/n per layer; PP: one bsh hop per stage boundary)?
predict.why: TP: 8 bsh x 7/8 = 7 bsh per layer (the 8 already counts forward and backward) x 32 layers = 224 bsh. PP: one bsh activation forward and one bsh gradient backward per stage boundary x 7 boundaries = 14 bsh (slide 43 gives bsh per microbatch per hop). 224/14 = 16. The gap grows with depth, and TP's traffic is in blocking all-reduces rather than point-to-point sends.
predict.targets_misconception: Tensor parallel is the better scheme in every respect since it has no bubble; pipeline parallel is a fallback for people who cannot wrap their model.

transfer.q: With b = 4, s = 4096, h = 8192 and n_devices = 8, compute (in elements) the per-layer tensor-parallel communication 8bsh(n-1)/n and the per-micro-batch pipeline communication bsh.
transfer.answer: bsh = 4 x 4096 x 8192 = 134,217,728 elements (PP per micro-batch per hop). TP per layer = 8 x 134,217,728 x 7/8 = 939,524,096 elements, 7x the PP figure for every single layer.
transfer.why: Both scale with activation size, not parameter count, so unlike ZeRO they do not grow with model width beyond h. The factor 8(n-1)/n approaches 8 for large n, so TP's per-layer cost is about an order of magnitude above a PP hop.

check.q: Using slide 43's formulas, with n_devices = 4, the per-layer tensor-parallel traffic 8bsh(n − 1)/n is how many times the activation size bsh that one pipeline hop moves?
check.why: 8 × 3/4 = 6: every tensor-parallel layer moves 6 activation-sized tensors, while a pipeline stage boundary moves one per micro-batch, which is why TP is confined to fast intra-node links.
check.varies: device count (4) and no concrete b, s, h, so the answer is a pure ratio
check.invariant: TP traffic per layer = 8bsh(n − 1)/n; a PP hop = bsh
check.targets_misconception: Tensor parallel is the better scheme in every respect since it has no bubble; pipeline parallel is a fallback for people who cannot wrap their model.

retrieval.q: Give the deck's per-layer communication for tensor parallel and the per-micro-batch communication for pipeline parallel.
retrieval.answer: Tensor: 8bsh(n_devices-1)/n_devices in all-reduces per layer. Pipeline: bsh point-to-point per micro-batch.

retrieval.q: Besides having no bubble, what two advantages of tensor parallel over pipeline parallel does the deck list?
retrieval.answer: Low complexity (simple to wrap models) and no need for large batch sizes.

retrieval.q: Which link does the deck assign to pipeline parallel and which to tensor parallel?
retrieval.answer: Pipeline on slower inter-node links; tensor parallel within a node on low-latency high-bandwidth interconnects (up to 8 GPUs).

steps.why: The 8 is 2 all-reduces per layer (attention and MLP) × 2 (forward and backward) × 2 (a ring all-reduce moves about twice the tensor); (n − 1)/n is the ring's share.

knowledge_points.label: Activation memory per layer: sbh(34 + 5as/h), and what TP cannot shrink
knowledge_points.statement: Storing everything, a Transformer layer's activations take sbh(34 + 5 as/h) bytes, the 5as/h part being the quadratic attention terms (droppable by recomputation as in FlashAttention); tensor parallel divides the matmul-related terms by t but leaves a 10 sbh floor from LayerNorm (4sbh), dropout (2sbh) and the inputs to attention and MLP (4sbh), which keeps growing with model size.

anchors.quote: Memory isn’t just the static bits, but also activations! This can be big
Tensor and pipeline parallel can linearly reduce those..but what about activations?

Starting point: activation memory needed if storing everything ... The 5 ... terms come from the quadratic attention terms incl dropout ... As with flash attention, we can drop this term via recomputation
Tensor parallel splits out the matrix multiplies in attention + MLP
The remaining 10 term is for the LayerNorm (4sbh), Dropout (2sbh), and inputs to the attention and MLP (4sbh). These terms alone will continue to grow with size
There's a lot of dynamic memory that needs to exist in a computation. ... And so really maximum memory usage happens a little bit after the maximum activation point.

as you go to bigger models, for moderately large sequence lengths, your activations are just going to dwarf the parameter memory that you need. And so any memory saving strategy has to reason about activations
the amount of activations that we need is going to be something like 34 times s times b times h ... plus 5 times as over h.
And this sbh dependence, right, is fundamental, because we expect to have to store something for every element of the sequence.
Well, the MLPs are 24 of those 34 that I talked about before. And the attention heads are 5 as over ht. ... Now, I can reduce that by t, my tensor parallel size.

You need to keep the inputs to attention and the MLP. Right, because the inputs to each layers need to be stored as residuals for the backwards pass. ... you're still going to suffer a 10 times sbh penalty

provenance.filtering_note: Both formulas are images: 'Activations memory per layer = sbh(34 + 5as/h)' on p46 and 'sbh(10 + 24/t + 5as/(ht))' on p47 are from Korthikanti et al. 2022 (equations 2 and 3, in bytes with 2-byte activations and 1-byte dropout masks). Only '5 as/h', '10 term', '4sbh', '2sbh', '4sbh' survive in the text layer; the coefficients 34 and 24 and the variable legend (a heads, b micro-batch, h hidden, L layers, p pipeline size, s sequence, t tensor size, v vocab) are figure-only. The deck does not derive 34 (it is the sum of the per-sublayer input, QKV, attention output, MLP and dropout-mask tensors). predict.q: A Transformer layer with s = 2048, h = 12288 and a = 96 heads stores sbh(34 + 5as/h) of activations. you have to incorporate MP, in this case, is tensor parallel, to the mix. Right, now you can push that curve out a little bit more and be compute bound even into smaller batch size regimes

misconceptions.belief: Bigger models make FSDP communication-bound, because there are more parameters to gather every step.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each chip's compute grows with the parameter count too (about 6 x N x its tokens), so N cancels: the ratio depends only on tokens per chip and the chip's FLOP/s over its link bandwidth.

misconceptions.belief: Once the model fits, FSDP's communication is always hidden by overlapping it with compute.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Overlap hides communication only when the compute takes at least as long. With few tokens per chip the all-gathers take longer than the layer's compute, and the difference shows up as idle time.

predict.q: An FSDP-only job is just compute-bound. Holding the chips, the network and the tokens per chip fixed, you double the model's parameter count. Does the minimum tokens-per-chip at which FSDP alone stays compute-bound go up, down or stay the same? Answer up, down or same.
predict.answer: same: doubling N doubles both each chip's compute (6 x N x tokens) and its FSDP traffic (about 3 x N x 2 bytes), so the threshold, chip FLOP/s over link bytes/s in tokens, does not move.
predict.why: Compute time is 6N x tokens / C and FSDP communication time is about 6N / W, so their ratio is tokens x W / C. The parameter count cancels. This is why the professor's plot has batch size per chip, not model size, on its axis.
predict.targets_misconception: Bigger models make FSDP communication-bound, because there are more parameters to gather every step.

transfer.q: Chips deliver C = 1e15 FLOP/s. Your FSDP group spans nodes, so its collectives run at W = 5e10 bytes/s per chip. The global batch is 4,194,304 tokens over 1,024 chips. Is FSDP alone compute-bound? Following the professor's advice, what would you add, and does 8-way tensor parallelism inside each node fix it (ignoring tensor parallelism's own traffic on the fast link)?
transfer.answer: No. The threshold is C/W = 1e15/5e10 = 20,000 tokens per chip, and each chip has 4,194,304/1,024 = 4,096, so communication takes about 5x longer than compute. Add tensor (model) parallelism inside the node: with t = 8 each chip gathers only N/8 of the parameters, so the threshold falls to 20,000/8 = 2,500 tokens per chip, and 4,096 is now above it, so FSDP traffic is hidden.
transfer.why: The ratio is t x (tokens per chip) x W / C. Slow inter-node links raise C/W tenfold compared with NVLink-class links, which is why FSDP alone stops scaling and model parallelism is added inside the fast domain, the 'push that curve out' move.
transfer.varies: slower links (inter-node) and a fixed global batch over many chips, then adding tensor parallelism
transfer.invariant: compute-bound iff t x tokens per chip x W > C; the parameter count cancels

check.q: An FSDP-only job runs on chips with C = 1e15 FLOP/s and collectives at W = 4.5e11 bytes/s, with 1,024 tokens per chip per step. Taking compute as 6 x N x tokens FLOPs and FSDP traffic as 3 x N x 2 bytes, by what factor does communication time exceed compute time? Type only the number.
check.why: Communication / compute = (6N/W) / (6N x 1024 / C) = C / (1024 x W) = 1e15 / 4.608e14, about 2.17. The threshold is C/W, about 2,222 tokens per chip, so at 1,024 the job waits on the network, in line with the professor's 'about 2,000 per chip' reading.
check.targets_misconception: Once the model fits, FSDP's communication is always hidden by overlapping it with compute.
check.varies: diagnosing how far below the threshold a job sits, on fast links, instead of deciding a fix
check.invariant: communication/compute = C / (tokens per chip x W) for FSDP alone

retrieval.q: What one quantity decides whether FSDP alone can hide its communication, and what is the threshold?
retrieval.answer: Tokens (batch) per chip. FSDP is compute-bound when tokens per chip exceed chip FLOP/s divided by link bytes/s; the professor's plot puts it at about 2,000 per chip.

retrieval.q: What did the professor say to add when the per-chip batch falls below FSDP's threshold, and why does it help?
retrieval.answer: Model (tensor) parallelism. Each chip then gathers only its 1/t slice of the parameters for the same compute, so the compute-bound region extends to about t times fewer tokens per chip.

knowledge_points.label: 3D parallelism recipe: TP/EP in-node, PP across nodes, then DP
knowledge_points.statement: Rule of thumb: until the model fits in memory, use tensor / expert parallel up to the GPUs per machine and pipeline parallel across machines (or ZeRO-3, depending on bandwidth); then scale the rest of the way with data parallel, gradient-accumulating if the batch is small; in Narayanan 2021 TP goes to 8 and caps there, PP grows to make the model fit, and DP shrinks from 32 to 6 for the largest model, and on 64 GPUs the (PP, TP) = (8, 8) configuration is best.

anchors.quote: 1. Until your model fits in memory.. ... Tensor / expert parallel up to GPUs / machine ... Pipeline parallel across machines ... (Or use Zero-3, depending on BW)
2. Then until you run out of GPUs ... Scale the rest of the way with data parallel
If your batch size is small.. gradient accumulate to trade higher batch sizes for better communication efficiency.
Tensor parallel first up to 8, then caps out at 8. ... Pipeline parallel goes up to make the model fit. ... Dara parallel gradually decreases with scale, with the largest model having DP=6
When parallelizing across 64 machines – it’s best to use a 8 x 8 configuration.
More GPUS, same, flat utilization!

anchors.ref: Narayanan et al. 2021, Table 1, Fig. 10, Fig. 13

anchors.quote: there is no one strictly dominant parallelization strategy. It's all a whole bunch of tradeoffs that you somehow have to manage gracefully

the strategy for how you parallelize is very simple, actually. Which is, until your model fits into memory, you're going to cut up your model by whatever means necessary ... And once your model fits, then you're going to just data parallel the rest of the way.

if you have eight GPUs per machine, you're going to use a tensor expert parallel of eight. And then you're going to pipeline parallel or Zero-3, which is FSDP, the rest of the way to make your model fit.

you see exactly the thing that I said, but in reverse order. So guideline number one is minimize model parallelism, maximize data parallelism. ... And then if you're going to go multi-node, use pipeline parallelism to go multi-node.
you have data parallel maxed out. And then your tensor parallel increases until it hits 8, and then you stop because you don't want to go any higher. ... And at the very end, you have a DP of six.
even as you go to ludicrously large numbers of GPUs, your utilization stays very flat and very good.

for different batch sizes for tensor parallel, what is the right place to stop? And it's clearly tensor parallel size of 8. ... And the larger the pipeline parallel, the larger the gap between orange and blue.

if you do activation recomputation very cleverly, then you can get a bigger batch size, and the bigger batch size then allows you to get better utilization. ... because it allows you to save memory, and memory can be turned into batch size.

misconceptions.belief: Model parallelism is what you scale when you get more GPUs; data parallel is the small-scale default.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The recipe uses only as much model parallelism (TP in-node, PP across nodes) as is needed to fit the model, then spends every remaining GPU on data parallel. Extra model parallelism beyond fit costs bubbles and communication for no memory benefit.

predict.q: You have 1024 GPUs in 8-GPU nodes. The model fits only with TP = 8 and PP = 4. Following the slide-57 recipe, what data-parallel degree do you end up with?
predict.why: TP x PP = 32 GPUs per model replica, and 'then until you run out of GPUs, scale the rest of the way with data parallel': 1024 / 32 = 32 replicas. Nothing else is increased once the model fits.
predict.targets_misconception: Model parallelism is what you scale when you get more GPUs; data parallel is the small-scale default.

transfer.q: Same 1024 GPUs and TP = 8, PP = 4, DP = 32, but your experiments require a global batch of only 256 sequences. The pipeline (slide 34) wants many micro-batches per replica. How many sequences does each replica see per step, and what does slide 57 say to do about the small batch?
transfer.answer: 256 / 32 = 8 sequences per replica per step, far too few micro-batches for a 4-stage pipeline (bubble ratio 3/m is huge). Slide 57: gradient accumulate, trading a higher effective batch for better communication efficiency (or reduce DP and accept idle GPUs).
transfer.why: Every data-parallel replica needs enough micro-batches to fill its pipeline and amortise its communication; when the batch cannot be divided that finely, accumulating steps is the lever the deck names.

check.q: 512 GPUs in 8-GPU nodes; following slide 57, the model fits with TP = 8 inside each node and PP = 8 across nodes, and the rest is data parallel. With a global batch of 1,024 sequences, how many sequences does each data-parallel replica process per step?
check.why: DP = 512 / (8 × 8) = 8 replicas, so each sees 1024 / 8 = 128 sequences, enough micro-batches to keep an 8-stage pipeline's bubble small (7/128 if each sequence is a micro-batch).
check.varies: GPU count, PP degree and batch size; the replica batch is large here rather than too small
check.invariant: TP × PP is fixed by what makes the model fit; DP takes the remaining GPUs and divides the batch
